item.title: open-webui/open-webui
item.description:
User-friendly AI Interface (Supports Ollama, OpenAI API, ...)

https://openwebui.com

Open WebUI

Open WebUI is a home for AI: an extensible, easy-to-use, self-hosted platform built to run entirely offline. Connect local models through Ollama, use OpenAI-compatible APIs for local and cloud models, or add agents through Agent Client Protocol (ACP).

English | 简体中文 | 繁體中文 | 한국어 | Deutsch | Español | Français | Italiano | Dansk | 日本語 | Polski | Русский | Bosanski | العربية | Norsk | Português (Brasil) | ไทย | Türkçe | Українська | বাংলা | Ελληνικά | Tiếng Việt

Explore Open WebUI →

Installation

Python

# With uv installed (macOS/Linux)
DATA_DIR=~/.open-webui uvx --python 3.12 open-webui@latest serve

# Or install and run with pip (Python 3.12)
pip install open-webui
open-webui serve

Then open http://localhost:8080.

Docker

docker run -d -p 3000:8080 --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway -v open-webui:/app/backend/data --name open-webui --restart always ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:main

Then open http://localhost:3000.

Image tag Includes
:main Standard image with local AI dependencies
:slim Lightweight image using external services for embeddings, document extraction, and voice
:cuda Open WebUI with CUDA acceleration
:ollama Open WebUI bundled with Ollama
:dev Latest development build

Add these options to docker run before the image name as needed:

Option Purpose
-e OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://your-ollama-server:11434 Connect to Ollama on another server
-e OPENAI_API_KEY=your_secret_key Set your OpenAI API key
-e HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 Disable Hugging Face model downloads for offline use
--gpus all Enable Nvidia GPU access for :cuda or :ollama; requires the Nvidia Container Toolkit

See the Docker installation guide for setup instructions and configuration options.

Desktop App

Download the native desktop app for macOS, Windows, and Linux.

Read the docs →

Ecosystem

  • Open Terminal / Terminals (Enterprise): The action layer that turns Open WebUI into a full agent harness, with enterprise orchestration for per-user workspaces.
  • Knowledge Base Sync (oikb): Mirror folders, repos, buckets, and wikis into Open WebUI Knowledge Bases with incremental sync.
  • Open WebUI Computer: Your computer in any browser: files, editor, terminal, git, and optional AI agents, running on your real machine.

See the ecosystem documentation for details.

Troubleshooting and Updates

See the troubleshooting guide for connection issues and the updating guide to update your installation.

Documentation

See the docs for configuration and usage, and the roadmap for planned work.

For Docker Compose, Kubernetes, and other setups, see the installation docs.

Support

Open an issue or start a discussion.

Find us on Reddit, X, and Discord.

Security

Report vulnerabilities privately through GitHub security advisories. Security reports are accepted only through GitHub.

Star History

License

Includes code under the Open WebUI License, which requires preserving the Open WebUI branding, and prior contributions under their original licenses. See LICENSE and LICENSE_HISTORY for terms and history.

Enterprise · Careers · Sponsor

Created by Timothy Jaeryang Baek.

item.title: open-webui/desktop
item.description:
Open WebUI Desktop 🌐

https://openwebui.com

Open WebUI Desktop

Open WebUI, up and running in a few clicks. Desktop installs it on your computer, keeps it up to date, and opens it whenever you need it.

Download

  • macOS: Apple Silicon · Intel
  • Windows: Intel / AMD (x64) · ARM64
  • Linux (Debian / Ubuntu / Mint): Intel / AMD (x64) · ARM64
  • Linux (AppImage): Intel / AMD (x64) · ARM64

If an AppImage fails to start with a chrome-sandbox error on Debian, Ubuntu, or Linux Mint, install the .deb package above. Its installer configures the sandbox permissions needed to start the app.

Snap and Flatpak packages are available on the releases page.

Internet is required for installation and updates.

Enable Automatic desktop updates in Settings → About to update on quit.

How It Works

Open the app and click Get Started. Desktop installs Open WebUI on your computer, starts it for you, and opens it in the app. You use the same Open WebUI you know, with setup and updates handled through Desktop.

Desktop runs your own local copy of Open WebUI. If you already use Open WebUI on another server, Open WebUI Tether is a companion app that extends what you can do with it.

System Requirements

Requirements
Disk 5 GB+
OS macOS 12+, Windows 10+, modern Linux (glibc 2.28+)

Privacy

Desktop does not collect usage data. If you connect Open WebUI to an external AI provider, that provider's privacy policy applies.

Community

  • 💬 Discord - Come hang out
  • 🐛 Issues - Report bugs or request features
  • 🌐 Open WebUI - The main project
  • 📖 Docs - Full documentation

Contributing

npm install
npm run dev

See CHANGELOG.md for release history. Licensed under AGPL-3.0.

item.title: Abdenasser/neohtop
item.description:
💪🏻 Blazing-fast system monitoring for your desktop (built with Rust, Tauri & Svelte)

https://abdenasser.github.io/neohtop/

NeoHtop

Your system. In plain sight.

A modern, open-source system monitor for macOS, Linux and Windows.
Explore processes, understand your graphics card, and keep your whole machine in view.

Download NeoHtop · Website · What’s new · Screenshots · Desktop guide

Catppuccin, front and center. 23 more themes when you want a change. Free, local, and open source.

Meet NeoHtop 1.3

A fresh desktop experience with more to explore—from the process holding a port to the GPU doing the work.

  • Go beyond a flat process list. Expand process families, see their combined CPU and RAM, and keep matching children in context while you search.
  • See your graphics card. GPU utilization, memory and driver-reported diagnostics sit alongside CPU, RAM, storage, system and network readings.
  • Keep the essentials in your menu bar. A compact companion shows live resources and your busiest processes. Jump straight into an inspector without hunting through the table.
  • Put a name to the process. Native app icons when the system can provide them; the familiar ghost when it can’t.
  • Find what owns a port. Type :3000 or port:443. Socket scans run only when you need them.
  • Keep the themes you love. All 24 themes, rebuilt around consistent shadcn-svelte controls, readable tokens, and a searchable gallery.

Read the complete v1.3.0 changelog →


Go deeper from every resource card.
CPU cores, memory breakdowns, graphics adapters, mounted volumes, system identity and network interfaces.
Your setup, your atmosphere.
Dark, light, colorful, retro and accessible palettes. The same theme follows you across app windows.

A whole monitor in your menu bar.

Open. Check. Carry on.

Your essential readings, without bringing the full app forward.

  • CPU, memory, GPU, network and free storage.
  • Your five busiest processes, with native icons.
  • One click from a process to its inspector.
  • Shared pause, sampling interval and theme.
  • Optional monitoring after closing the main window.

Explore the companion →

Real macOS system capture. Also available through the system tray on supported desktops.

Less hunting. More understanding.

What you’re looking for Where to start
A process eating CPU or RAM Sort the table, filter by usage, pin it, or open its inspector.
What belongs to an app Switch to Tree and expand its process family.
The server holding your dev port Search :3000 or port:443. A bare number still finds a PID.
GPU load and memory Open Graphics from the GPU card; select an adapter on multi-GPU machines.
A sudden resource spike Inspect the CPU, memory, GPU or network chart with the pointer or keyboard.
Traffic on a particular interface Open Network, search interfaces, or include inactive ones.
A quick check between tasks Open the ghost in the menu bar/system tray.
Your preferred monitoring pace Open Settings → General and choose a refresh interval.

The charts keep roughly two minutes of history in memory. Pause, inspect and resume from the app bar or companion; both windows share the same sample and monitoring state.

Download

Official packages are published on GitHub Releases, with SHA-256 checksums and a build manifest.

Platform Packages
macOS · Apple Silicon DMG
macOS · Intel DMG
Windows · x64 Installer
Linux · x86_64 deb · rpm · AppImage
Linux · ARM64 deb · rpm · AppImage

Installation and troubleshooting →

Prefer a community package manager?

Community packages are maintained independently and can update on a different schedule from official releases.

Platform Command
Homebrew brew install --cask neohtop
Arch Linux / AUR yay -S neohtop or paru -S neohtop
Fedora / Terra dnf install neohtop after enabling Terra
Windows / Scoop scoop bucket add extras, then scoop install extras/neohtop
Solus eopkg install neohtop

A few details worth knowing

Search, filters and process families

Search names, commands and PIDs. Commas match any term; regular expressions work too: node, python, d$, or ^kernel. Use Filters to combine CPU, GPU engine activity, RAM, runtime and status conditions. Clear active conditions in one action.

Tree mode keeps parent context around matches and pages whole families together. Family CPU can exceed 100% across cores; summed resident RAM can double-count shared pages. List mode keeps individual process readings. View controls columns, and the bottom bar controls page size.

GPU support depends on your platform and driver
Platform Driver sources
macOS IORegistry utilization and available Apple silicon shared-memory/core data.
Linux AMD amdgpu sysfs and NVIDIA NVML; DRM inventory for other adapters.
Windows NVIDIA NVML; DXGI inventory and reported dedicated capacity for other adapters.

Temperature, power, clock and other counters appear only where exposed. Unsupported or unreadable values stay unavailable. Shared GPU memory on Apple silicon is already part of system RAM.

Optional GPU % process columns and filters use Linux DRM engine accounting. They need a baseline and can exceed 100% across engines; they are different from the device’s normalized utilization. Collection runs only when the column or filter is enabled. Socket visibility also depends on OS permissions; the app does not request elevation automatically.

Settings, shortcuts and the menu-bar companion
  • ⌘F / Ctrl+F: focus process search.
  • ⌘, / Ctrl+,: open Settings. General holds refresh/tray behavior; Appearance holds themes.
  • Escape: clear search when focused, or dismiss an open detail sheet.
  • Chart arrow keys: inspect recorded samples.

The companion shows CPU, RAM, GPU, network, free storage and the five busiest processes. Select a process to inspect it in the main app. It stops polling while hidden. On some Linux desktops, use the tray menu’s Show overview command or the app-bar button.

Closing the main window quits by default. Enable Keep running when the window closes to continue from the tray. Closing Settings/About leaves monitoring running; Quit NeoHtop always exits. Preferences save automatically and migrate from existing local settings.

Build with us

NeoHtop is built with Rust + Tauri + Svelte, with shadcn-svelte + Tailwind CSS for shared controls and all 24 original themes. Native process icons use platform providers, with Lucide for interface controls.

git clone https://github.com/Abdenasser/neohtop.git
cd neohtop
npm ci
npm run tauri dev

Use Node.js 22, Rust 1.88+, and the Tauri prerequisites for your OS.

Development and release guide · Contributing · Report a bug · Migration notes

Prefer your terminal?

Meet NeoHtop CLI, the separate Go/Charm companion with process trees, CPU sparklines, memory bars, filters and themes.

npm install -g neohtop-cli

Desktop vs CLI →

Free today. Open source at the core.

This release is the free, MIT-licensed desktop app. No account or cloud subscription is required. NeoHtop Pro is postponed and is not available to buy or install; no launch date or pricing is announced.

If NeoHtop earns a place in your setup, star the project, sponsor development, or buy Abdenasser a coffee.

The story behind NeoHtop · MIT License

Privacy and analytics

Official v1.3.0 builds send a basic launch count and app version without a persistent identifier, even when optional sharing is off. Settings → Privacy lets you opt in to limited feature usage. Process names, search text, commands, paths and system readings stay local. See the privacy notice.

item.title: satisfactorymodding/SatisfactoryModManager
item.description:
A mod manager for easy installation of mods and modloader for Satisfactory

https://docs.ficsit.app/satisfactory-modding/latest/ForUsers/Welcome.html

Satisfactory Mod Manager

Mod manager for Satisfactory. Handles all the steps of installing mods for you.

Implemented in Wails using Svelte and Skeleton.

Installation and Usage

Check the modding documentation for installation and usage instructions.

Features

  • One-click install of any mod
  • Automatically downloads the dependencies of any mod
  • Mod update notifications
  • Mod profiles and sharing of them
  • View the mod description in the app

Reporting issues

If you have any questions or run into issues, you can ask in the Satisfactory Modding discord for quicker responses than the GitHub issues. If there is any error message, please include it along with the generated debug info zip.

Troubleshooting

Check the modding documentation for common issues and their solutions.

  • Profile and installation records are located in %APPDATA%\ficsit\
  • Downloads are cached in %LOCALAPPDATA%\ficsit\downloadCache\
  • Logs are stored in %LOCALAPPDATA%\SatisfactoryModManager\logs

Development

Dependencies

  • Go (the version in the Setup CI action go-version)
  • pnpm
  • nodejs (the version in the Setup CI action node-version)
  • Wails (to install, execute the run command from the Setup CI action's Install Wails step)
  • IDE of Choice. Goland or VSCode suggested.

Configuration

If you want to point to the SMR staging API instead of production, edit:

  • main.go to set api-base to the staging api (https://api.ficsit.dev)
  • frontend\.graphqlrc.yml to set schema to the staging api (https://api.ficsit.dev/v2/query)

If you want to use a local build of ficsit-cli, use the Go replace directive (and do not commit the change), for example:

go mod edit -replace github.com/satisfactorymodding/ficsit-cli=C:\Git\ficsit-cli

Development Server

The development server will hot reload whenever you make changes to the Go or Typescript code.

wails dev

Upon successful launch of the development server, the application will open automatically. The command line output will also include a localhost URL you can visit in your browser if you wish to utilize browser developer tools for debugging.

Make sure you don't already have a copy of the application running or the command will silently fail.

Although wails dev should run these commands for you under normal circumstances, you may need to run pnpm graphql-codegen in the frontend directory to update the code generated from the SMR API, or run pnpm translations to update the translation data.

IDE Configuration

Make sure that your IDE is connecting with the frontend's installation of ESLint to get the best experience.

VSCode users, a preconfigured workspace is provided in .vscode/ that allows editing both Go and Svelte files while maintaining correct ESLint functionality.

Building

wails build

To build a version that includes browser devtools (extending production debugging capabilities),:

wails build -devtools

Linting

Install golangci-lint via the directions in the Golangci-lint documentation, but make sure to install the version specified in .github/workflows/push.yaml instead of whatever it suggests.

Then, to run it, use:

golangci-lint run --fix

You may also need to manually run the frontend linter. First, navigate to the frontend directory, then run:

pnpm run format
pnpm run check

Assorted Development Helpers

  • Browser dev tools should automatically open when running wails dev.
  • You can open the URL the frontend is being served on in a browser to use browser extensions like the Svelte Devtools. Check the logs for Using DevServer URL: to find the correct URL.
  • You can manually trigger an error popup for testing purposes by running debugCauseErrorMessage("your message here") in the devtools console.

Localization

If you'd like to help translate and localize SMM to different languages, join our discord server.

SMM handles localization through the Tolgee Svelte integration. This allows for in-context translation - simply alt-click on a translatable element to open the Tolgee interface.

In order to edit translations in-context, you will need to provide a tolgee API key with edit permissions. You can create an API key for yourself in our Tolgee instance once you're added to the project. To supply this API key at development time, create or edit /frontend/.env.local and supply the key in a similar format as .env.

The in-context translation screenshot feature requires installing the Tolgee Tools browser extension. After running wails dev, open http://localhost:34115/ in your browser of choice to access the application.

Code Signing Policy

Free code signing provided by SignPath.io, certificate by SignPath Foundation
Committers and reviewers Approvers Privacy Policy
Organization members Owners https://ficsit.app/privacy-policy

item.title: leaningtech/webvm
item.description:
Virtual Machine for the Web

https://webvm.io

WebVM

This repository hosts the source code for https://webvm.io, a Linux virtual machine that runs in your browser.

Try out the new Alpine / Xorg / i3 graphical environment: https://webvm.io/alpine.html

What is WebVM?

WebVM is a server-less virtual environment running fully client-side in HTML5/WebAssembly. It's designed to be Linux ABI-compatible and runs an unmodified Debian distribution including many native development toolchains.

WebVM is powered by the CheerpX virtualization engine, which provides:

  • x86-to-WebAssembly JIT compiler
  • Virtual block-based file system
  • Linux syscall emulator
  • Safe, sandboxed client-side execution

Table of Contents

  • Networking
  • Development & Customization
    • Deploy to GitHub Pages
    • Local Serving & Image Configuration
  • Claude AI Integration
  • Community & Support
  • Learn More
  • License

Note

Visit https://webvm.io to get started immediately in your browser. No setup required.

For local setup, custom image builds, and fork/deploy guidance, see Development & Customization.

Networking

WebVM supports Tailscale integration. So your browser VM can reach your private network and, with an exit node, the public internet too.

Note

Some low-level networking operations (especially ICMP used by ping) are not currently available in this environment. For connectivity checks, use curl or wget.

Local network

  1. Open the "Networking" panel from the sidebar
  2. Click "Connect to Tailscale"
  3. Log in (create a free account at tailscale.com if needed)
  4. Click "Connect" when prompted

WebVM now has access to all machines in your Tailscale network!

Internet Usage Tips

Tip

On slower connections there may be a short delay before initialisation. Connection status is shown as a colored dot on the button: orange = local network, green = global/internet. The button text shows your Tailscale IP address once connected.

To access the public internet from WebVM, set up an Exit Node on another device in your Tailscale network:

  1. Follow the Tailscale Exit Node quickstart (sections: "Advertise a device as an exit node")
  2. WebVM automatically uses the exit node once advertised

Using an Auth Key

As an alternative to interactive login, add your Tailscale auth key to the URL fragment:

https://webvm.io/#authKey=<your-ephemeral-key>

This is equivalent to Tailscale's --login-server option.

Tip

If you also need a custom control server, add controlUrl in the same URL fragment and separate values with &, for example: #authKey=...&controlUrl=....

Self-Hosting Tailscale with Headscale

We also support headscale, a selfhosted open source implementation of the Tailscale control server. Because Headscale does not add CORS headers by default, you will need a proxy in front of it. See the Headscale reverse proxy setup docs for an example.

Once ready, add the following line to your location / block in your nginx config file.

if ($http_origin = "https://yourdomain.com") {
    add_header 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' "$http_origin";
    add_header 'Access-Control-Allow-Credentials' 'true' always;
}

Then access WebVM with:

https://yourdomain.com/#controlUrl=<your-headscale-url>

Development & Customization

Note

Users have root privileges by default. sudo is not installed though this can easily be added to the Dockerfile if needed.

Deploy to GitHub Pages

This is a simple, beginner-friendly workflow. For local hosting and customization, see below Local Serving & Image Configuration.

Fork the WebVM repository to deploy your own version to GitHub Pages:

  1. Fork the repository
  2. Enable GitHub Pages via forked repository in Settings → Pages using "GitHub Actions" as source
  3. Run the Deploy workflow from Actions
  4. After completion, open the URL shown under the deploy_to_github_pages job

The same Deploy workflow also builds custom .ext2 disk images from a Dockerfile. You can point it at dockerfiles/debian_mini or another Dockerfile, then either publish the result as a GitHub Release asset or deploy the Pages build from your fork.

Note

dockerfiles/debian_large is too large of an image for GitHub pages.

Local Serving & Image Configuration

1. Clone the repository

git clone https://github.com/leaningtech/webvm.git
cd webvm

2. Put your image in custom-disk-images/

This repository includes a persistent custom-disk-images/ directory for local .ext2 files.

To use the official Debian mini image, download it from Releases:

debian_mini_20230519_5022088024.ext2

You can also copy in an image you built yourself.

3. Point WebVM to your local image

Edit config_public_terminal.js:

export const diskImageUrl =
  "/custom-disk-images/debian_mini_20230519_5022088024.ext2";
export const diskImageType = "bytes";

4. Install dependencies and build

npm install
npm run build

5. Start Nginx and open WebVM

nginx -p . -c nginx.conf

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8081 and enjoy your local WebVM!

For the full Alpine desktop environment, see leaningtech/alpine-image.

For more details, see CheerpX Custom Images documentation.

Tip

For Python3 REPL, the Deploy workflow takes into account the CMD specified in the Dockerfile.

To build a REPL you can simply change CMD [ "/bin/bash" ] to CMD [ "/usr/bin/python3" ] and deploy.

Claude AI Integration

To access Claude AI, you need an API key. Follow these steps to get started:

1. Create an account

  • Visit Anthropic Console and sign up with your e-mail. You'll receive a sign in link to the Anthropic Console.

2. Get your API key

  • Once logged in, navigate to Get API keys.
  • Purchase the amount of credits you need. After completing the purchase, you'll be able to generate the key through the API console.

3. Log in with your API key

  • Navigate to your WebVM and hover over the robot icon. This will show the Claude AI Integration tab. For added convenience, you can click the pin button in the top right corner to keep the tab in place.
  • You'll see a prompt where you can insert your Claude API key.

4. Start using Claude AI

  • Once your API key is entered, you can begin interacting with Claude AI by asking questions such as:

"Solve the CTF challenge at /home/user/chall1.bin. Note that the binary reads from stdin."

Important: Your API key is private and should never be shared. We do not have access to your key, it is only stored locally in your browser.

Community & Support

Report issues: Use GitHub Issues to report bugs or request features.

Chat with us: Join our Discord community to discuss WebVM, share ideas, and get help.

Learn More

Articles & Resources:

  • WebVM: Server-less x86 virtual machines in the browser
  • WebVM: Linux Virtualization in WebAssembly with Full Networking via Tailscale
  • Mini.WebVM: Your own Linux box from Dockerfile, virtualized in the browser via WebAssembly
  • Crafting the Impossible: X86 Virtualization in the Browser with WebAssembly — Talk at JsNation 2022

Example Deployment:

  • Mini.WebVM Reference — A running example deployed to GitHub Pages

Technology Behind WebVM:

This project is powered by:

  • CheerpX — x86-to-WebAssembly JIT compiler | by Leaning Technologies
  • xterm.js — Web-based terminal emulator
  • Tailscale — VPN networking layer
  • lwIP — TCP/IP stack, compiled for the Web via Cheerp

Versioning:

WebVM uses the CheerpX NPM package, which is updated on every release.

Every build is immutable. If a specific version works well for you today, it will keep working forever.

You are welcome to use, modify, and redistribute the contents of this repository.

The public CheerpX deployment is provided as-is and is free to use for technological exploration, testing and use by individuals. Any other use by organizations, including non-profit, academia and the public sector, requires a license. Downloading a CheerpX build for the purpose of hosting it elsewhere is not permitted without a commercial license.

Read more here about our licensing practices.

If you want to build a product on top of CheerpX/WebVM, please see our other licensing options: CheerpX licensing or get in touch: sales@leaningtech.com
